position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home fitness or weight management) built on the stand-on bioelectrical impedance analyser, with a focus on accuracy and health messaging. Begin with a limited pilot in regions where health awareness is high to validate demand before broader rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must consider current consumer reach of Tanita's products and the competitive landscape.
Evidence must be from sources read before the decision date; later developments are not usable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or health monitoring).
2) Expand the existing commercial offering to additional clinic/health‑club segments without a consumer focus.
3) Maintain current product portfolio and not pursue any new consumer proposition (no expansion).
4) Pursue a different route to consumers (e.g., retail partnerships, online sales, or a new distribution channel) rather than a new product proposition.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it provides a clear, accurate, and easy-to-interpret measurement of body fat, because they need reliable health information for personal health management.
T1.who_benefits: Home users seeking to monitor body fat for health reasons (e.g., weight management, diabetes prevention).
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Current BIA devices are inaccurate and require technical expertise; a consumer-friendly, accurate device removes the barrier to self-monitoring.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge a premium for a consumer-branded, easy-to-use device sold directly or through retail partners, leveraging its existing brand recognition and manufacturing capabilities.
assumptions: Consumers value accuracy over cost in health-related measurements.
Retail distribution can reach target home users effectively.
The device's accuracy can be demonstrated to consumers through clear messaging.
predictions: If offered a consumer proposition, purchase intent among health-conscious home users will be higher than for a clinical-only device.
Sales will be concentrated in regions where health awareness is high and home use is feasible.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it provides a clear, accurate, and easy-to-interpret measurement of body fat, because they need reliable health information for personal health management.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a fashion accessory or status symbol, because they purchase health-related products for personal expression rather than functional health monitoring.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers who view health monitoring as part of lifestyle and status signaling.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A device marketed as a fashion item or status symbol creates a perceived social value beyond health data, prompting purchase even if accuracy is marginal.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing, limited-edition designs, and brand association with health and style, leveraging its existing consumer brand in Japan.
assumptions: Consumers associate health monitoring with personal style and status.
Fashion-driven marketing can overcome perceived accuracy concerns.
A limited-edition or design-focused offering can generate demand without heavy health messaging.
predictions: If marketed as a fashion item, purchase intent among style-conscious consumers will be higher than for a health-focused device.
Sales will be concentrated in regions where fashion and lifestyle branding are prominent.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a fashion accessory or status symbol, because they purchase health-related products for personal expression rather than functional health monitoring.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Health vs Fashion Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from health-conscious and fashion-conscious segments. In the Health condition, the device is described as a professional-grade body-fat analyser for home use, emphasizing accuracy and health benefits. In the Fashion condition, the device is described as a stylish, limited-edition accessory for personal expression. Both conditions include a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question.
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) from regions where health awareness is high (e.g., Japan) and fashion awareness is high (e.g., the US). Recruit via online panels to ensure diversity.
X1.measure: WTP in euros per device. Secondary measure: self-reported purchase intent on a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health condition WTP ≥ €30 and purchase intent ≥ 5; Fashion condition WTP ≤ €20.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Fashion condition WTP ≥ €30 and purchase intent ≥ 5; Health condition WTP ≤ €20.

X1.decision_rule: If the Health condition WTP ≥ €30 AND purchase intent ≥ 5 AND the Fashion condition WTP ≤ €20, proceed with a consumer proposition focused on health accuracy. If the Fashion condition WTP ≥ €30 AND purchase intent ≥ 5 AND the Health condition WTP ≤ €20, proceed with a fashion proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home fitness or weight management) built on the stand-on bioelectrical impedance analyser, with a focus on accuracy and health messaging. Begin with a limited pilot in regions where health awareness is high to validate demand before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious home users who need reliable body-fat information for personal health management.
final.value_proposition: A consumer-branded, easy-to-use body-fat analyser that delivers accurate, professional-grade results, leveraging Tanita’s existing brand recognition and manufacturing capabilities.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (Health vs Fashion messaging) to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the relative importance of accuracy versus fashion marketing are uncertain. Evidence shows the device is accurate for clinical use but does not address consumer motivation or purchase intent.
would_change_if: If the Consumer Proposition Test shows the Fashion condition WTP ≥ €30 and purchase intent ≥ 5, we would shift focus to a fashion-driven consumer proposition.
If new evidence shows the device is significantly less accurate for non-clinical users or that consumers prioritize other health monitoring methods, we would reconsider the investment.

X1.sample: 400 health-conscious adults (BMI 18-45) and 400 fitness-focused adults (BMI 18-45) recruited via panel, balanced across gender and region.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health messaging group will have higher purchase intent and WTP than fitness messaging group.

If both groups are equal, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health‑conscious individuals who seek ongoing body‑fat monitoring, supported by the medical evidence linking excess fat to chronic diseases and the company’s existing professional market presence.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must consider current consumer reach of Tanita's products and the competitive landscape.
Evidence must be from sources read before the decision date; later developments are not usable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or health monitoring).
2) Expand the existing commercial offering to additional clinic/health‑club segments without a consumer focus.
3) Maintain current product portfolio and not pursue any new consumer proposition (no expansion).
4) Pursue a different route to consumers (e.g., retail partnerships, online sales, or a new distribution channel) rather than a new product proposition.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a health and fitness necessity, leading them to purchase it for regular use rather than as a one‑time measurement.
T1.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking to monitor body fat for diet, exercise, and disease prevention.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of the link between excess body fat and chronic diseases creates a perceived health need; consumers will act on this need by purchasing a device that provides ongoing measurement.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing for a home device, repeat purchases for calibration/accessories, and brand extension as a health‑focused lifestyle brand.
assumptions: Consumers trust the accuracy of BIA technology for body‑fat estimation.
Health awareness is sufficient to drive purchase decisions in 1993.
Distribution channels (retail, online) can reach target consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a home body‑fat analyser to health‑conscious consumers, purchase intent or actual purchase rate will be higher than for a clinical‑only device.
Consumers will report higher perceived health benefit and willingness to pay compared to a clinical device.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a health and fitness necessity, leading them to purchase it for regular use rather than as a one‑time measurement.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a convenient, one‑time measurement for personal use, reducing the perceived need for ongoing health monitoring.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers seeking a quick, easy way to assess body fat without a subscription or regular clinic visits.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The convenience of a single measurement eliminates the need for repeated use, making the device attractive for one‑time health checks rather than daily monitoring.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through a lower‑priced, one‑time purchase model, reduced repeat purchase costs, and potential cross‑selling of accessories or calibration kits.
assumptions: Consumers value convenience and are willing to pay for a quick measurement.
The perceived health benefit is secondary to convenience in 1993 consumer decisions.
Distribution channels can reach consumers who prefer one‑time purchases.
predictions: In a test offering a home body‑fat analyser marketed as a one‑time measurement, purchase intent or actual purchase rate will be higher than for a health‑focused device.
Consumers will report higher convenience and lower perceived health need compared to a health‑focused device.

X1.sample: 500 adults (18-65) recruited via an online panel, stratified by health awareness (high vs low) and BMI (underweight vs overweight).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health‑conscious participants will show higher purchase intent and WTP than convenience‑focused participants.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience‑focused participants will show higher purchase intent and WTP than health‑conscious participants.

If the difference is less than 10 points, proceed with a convenience‑focused proposition. If both groups show similar intent, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health‑conscious individuals who seek ongoing body‑fat monitoring, supported by the medical evidence linking excess fat to chronic diseases and Tanita’s existing professional market presence.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious adults (18–65) who regularly monitor body fat for diet, exercise, and disease prevention.
final.value_proposition: A home body‑fat analyser that provides continuous, accurate body‑fat measurement, enabling users to track progress and make informed health decisions, positioned as a premium health‑focused lifestyle product.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week online survey test (500 participants, randomized messaging) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a health‑focused versus convenience‑focused offering.
final.uncertainty: The actual purchase behavior of consumers in 1993 is unknown; the test will resolve whether demand is driven by health need (T1) or convenience (T2).

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to 1993; no internal company data.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or health monitoring).

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser if it is marketed as a health‑monitoring device for home use, because they already keep track of body fat through bathroom scales and seek convenience and accuracy.
T1.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers (home users) who want to monitor body fat without clinic visits.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers perceive the device as a convenient, at‑home alternative to clinic measurements, they will purchase it for regular use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capturing margin through brand and retail distribution.
assumptions: Consumers trust home measurements for health monitoring.
Marketing can shift perception from clinical tool to consumer health device.
Distribution channels (retail, online) are available for home use.
predictions: A survey of 1,000 households would show >30% would purchase a stand‑on analyser if priced at €80-€120.
Sales in a pilot retail store would exceed 50 units per month within 3 months.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser if it is marketed as a health‑monitoring device for home use, because they already keep track of body fat through bathroom scales and seek convenience and accuracy.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser if it is marketed as a professional‑grade tool for health‑club and clinic use, because they trust clinical accuracy and seek validation for medical or fitness recommendations.
T2.who_benefits: Professional users (health clubs, clinics) who need reliable body‑fat data for client care.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If the device is positioned as a clinical tool with proven accuracy, professionals will recommend it to clients and purchase it for regular use.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device through B2B channels at higher volume prices, capturing margin through volume sales and professional distribution.

B2B distribution channels exist for health clubs and clinics.
predictions: A survey of 200 health‑club managers would show >40% would purchase the device if priced at €150‑€200 per unit.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: If the device reliably measures body fat and presents results in a clear, actionable format, consumers will be motivated to purchase it for regular home use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would capture value by selling a premium consumer version of its existing clinic/health‑club scale, leveraging its brand reputation and the existing BIA technology base.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance analyser if it is marketed as a convenient, one‑foot measurement that eliminates the need for multiple body parts and reduces measurement time, because they value speed and simplicity in health monitoring.
T2.who_benefits: Time‑constrained health‑conscious consumers who prefer quick, non‑invasive measurements over multiple body parts.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If the device provides a single, quick measurement of body fat without requiring the user to stand on two feet, consumers will be motivated to purchase it for its convenience and speed.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would capture value by offering a consumer version of its existing stand‑on analyser, positioning it as a faster, one‑foot alternative to traditional scales, and potentially commanding a premium price.

Marketing can effectively communicate the speed advantage to potential buyers.
predictions: In a test offering a one‑foot analyser to a sample of health‑conscious consumers, purchase intent will be higher than for a multi‑foot version.
Consumers will report higher satisfaction with the speed and convenience of the one‑foot measurement compared to traditional scales.

X1.method: Randomized controlled trial with two groups. Recruit 200 health-conscious adults (BMI 16-41 kg/m2) via an online panel. Randomly assign 100 to the accuracy group and 100 to the convenience group. Accuracy group receives a full stand-on BIA analyser with detailed body-fat results. Convenience group receives the same analyser but marketed as a one-foot, quick measurement. Both groups complete a 2‑week tracking task (record daily weight and mood). After 2 weeks, measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP).
X1.sample: 200 adults (100 accuracy, 100 convenience) screened for health‑conscious interest.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).

X1.decision_rule: If the accuracy group’s purchase intent is at least 5 percentage points higher than the convenience group and its WTP is at least €20 above the convenience group’s WTP, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing accuracy. position.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR's 406 MHz technology is approved for general public use and is already sold to private boat owners, but it does not demonstrate that private boat owners would purchase a consumer EPIRB or switch from ELTs. The $800 price point is supported by independent evidence, but demand remains unproven. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Insurance Messaging Test.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources available by late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must assess demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer use case.
Consider existing B2B products (shipping, aviation, military) and any potential new customer segments.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑focused product for a specific use case (e.g., marine safety for private boat owners).
2) Expand B2B offerings to new segments (e.g., commercial marine, aviation, or insurance companies).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B products and markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Partner with an established consumer brand to co‑develop a product.

T1.claim: Private boat owners will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz EPIRB if it is priced below $800 and marketed as a marine safety necessity, because they currently rely on expensive ELTs and face increasing liability and insurance costs.
T1.who_benefits: Private boat owners and their insurers who need reliable emergency communication.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They perceive a safety gap between current ELTs and the $800+ cost of a 406 MHz EPIRB, and would switch to a cheaper, satellite-based solution if it meets certification and reliability standards.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales at a premium price, and through potential insurance rate reductions if the device is proven to reduce claims.
assumptions: Private boat owners have sufficient disposable income to purchase a consumer EPIRB.
Regulatory certification allows consumer-grade 406 MHz devices to be marketed as marine safety equipment.
Insurance companies will offer discounts for devices that reduce emergency response times.
predictions: A survey of 500 private boat owners will show >30% would purchase a consumer EPIRB priced under $800.
Pilot sales of a consumer EPIRB will generate at least $50,000 in revenue within 6 months.
T1.first_claim: Private boat owners will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz EPIRB if it is priced below $800 and marketed as a marine safety necessity, because they currently rely on expensive ELTs and face increasing liability and insurance costs.

T2.claim: Insurance companies will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz EPIRB as a risk management tool to reduce claims and improve emergency response times, leading private boat owners to purchase it through their coverage providers.
T2.who_benefits: Insurance companies seeking to lower claim costs and improve customer safety.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Insurance companies evaluate safety devices as a cost-effective way to reduce claims and potentially lower premiums, and will recommend or subsidize devices that demonstrably reduce emergency response times.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR captures value through volume sales to insurers and potential premium discounts, and through data on claim reduction that can be used to justify higher prices.
assumptions: Insurance companies have the budget to subsidize or include safety devices in coverage.
A demonstrated reduction in emergency response times translates to measurable claim cost savings.
Regulatory certification allows insurers to recommend consumer EPIRBs as part of safety packages.
predictions: A survey of 200 insurance underwriters will show >40% would include a consumer EPIRB in coverage packages if it reduces claims by at least 10%.
Pilot sales of a subsidized consumer EPIRB will generate at least $100,000 in revenue within 6 months through insurance partnerships.

X1.name: Consumer vs Insurance Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 500 private boat owners (n=250) and 200 insurance underwriters (n=100). Randomly assign participants to one of two message groups: Group A receives a consumer-focused message emphasizing price ($799) and marine safety necessity; Group B receives an insurance-focused message emphasizing claim reduction and premium discounts. Both groups are shown a product description of a 406 MHz EPIRB. Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP).
X1.sample: 500 private boat owners (250 per group) and 200 insurance underwriters (100 per group).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group B because the consumer message directly addresses price sensitivity and safety need.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group A because insurance underwriters are motivated by cost savings and premium discounts.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent in Group A exceeds Group B by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 35% vs 25%), proceed to develop a consumer proposition. If purchase intent in Group B exceeds Group A by at least 10 percentage points, pursue insurance partnership. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test for Lawn Tractor
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay questions.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults aged 25-55 who have garden tasks (e.g., mowing, landscaping). Recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: 1) Willingness to pay a premium (percentage willing to pay at least 20% more for a Deere lawn tractor vs. a generic brand). 2) Primary reason for choosing (status/prestige vs. durability/reliability).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of respondents will choose the Deere lawn tractor for status/prestige reasons, and willingness to pay premium will be above 20%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 30% of respondents will choose the Deere lawn tractor for durability/reliability reasons, and willingness to pay premium will be above 15%.

arguments.decision_rule: If the share of respondents choosing status/prestige reasons exceeds the share choosing durability/reliability reasons by at least 5 percentage points, recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on status and premium pricing (favored theory T1). If the difference is less than 5 points, recommend further market research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping or gardening) built on Deere's tractor engineering, leveraging the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and existing dealers were selling other brands, but it does not demonstrate homeowner demand, willingness to pay a premium, or the recurring nature of lawn mowing. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to test T1 vs T2 before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-1962
No access to Deere's internal financial data or strategic plans
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeframe for any proposed experiment
Must consider the company's existing distribution network of independent dealers
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping, gardening, or light construction)
Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition
Maintain the current business model with no expansion (continue selling through independent dealers)
Target a different customer group (e.g., small farms, hobbyists, or urban property owners) rather than a specific use case

X1.decision_rule: If WTP for the John Deere lawn tractor exceeds the generic brand by at least 20% and is driven primarily by convenience/reliability (e.g., time savings, brand trust), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If neither threshold is met, maintain current model without expansion.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with a simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two product descriptions of a differentiated Deere lawn and garden tractor: one positioned as a status symbol (status) and one positioned as a specific, easy-to-use use case (specific). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase a single unit and at what price they would pay. The test also includes a control group viewing a generic lawn mower.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to reflect the target market.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the status positioning will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those viewing the specific positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the specific positioning will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those viewing the status positioning.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for the status positioning is at least 20% higher than for the specific positioning (i.e., status price ≥ specific price – 20%) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude that T1 is supported. If the specific positioning outperforms the status positioning and the difference is statistically significant, conclude that T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, neither theory is supported.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with a simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two product descriptions of a differentiated Deere lawn and garden tractor: one positioned as a status symbol (status) and one positioned as a specific, easy-to-use use case (specific). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase a single unit and at what price they would pay. The test also includes a control group viewing a generic lawn mower.
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to reflect the target market.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the status positioning will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those viewing the specific positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the specific positioning will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those viewing the status positioning.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for the status positioning is at least 20% higher than for the specific positioning (i.e., status price ≥ specific price – 20%) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude that T1 is supported. If the specific positioning outperforms the status positioning and the difference is statistically significant, conclude that T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, neither theory is supported.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.
